stem: Two centers report conflicting results for the **same** myocardial protection technique, each judged only by clinical outcomes. According to the chapter, how should the quality of myocardial management be **routinely assessed**?

choices.text: By hospital mortality and other overall clinical outcomes
By isolated cardiac parameters, such as intraoperative TEE return of septal contractility
By the time to ischemic contracture of the left ventricle
By the extent of the surgical incision and the number of transfusions
By the duration of postoperative sleep deprivation and noise exposure

explanation.text: Myocardial management **can and should be routinely assessed by isolated cardiac parameters** — e.g. ==intraoperative TEE return of septal contractility==, aortocoronary sinus enzyme measurements and cellular functional parameters.

steps.text: Clinical result = **sum of its parts** (preoperative energy status, anesthesia, extracorporeal circulation, organ protection, procedure length, transfusions, postoperative care)

steps.label: but
steps.text: Another step **cannot compensate** for an imperfect step (perfect protection cannot counteract imperfect surgical technique, and vice versa)
Much **variation** in results for the same technique, especially if **only clinical parameters** are used

explanation.caption: Operative phases critical for myocardial management (Fig. 3.1)
head: Phase
Factors
rows: Anesthesia, surgical incision, extracorporeal circulation, organ ischemia (e.g. myocardial management), surgical technique, transfusion
Transfusion, re-intervention, sleep deprivation, noise, drug interactions

explanation.text: Phase factors (incision, transfusions, sleep deprivation) **influence** cellular homeostasis; they are not measures of the quality of myocardial management.

The quality of myocardial management can and should be routinely assessed by isolated cardiac parameters, such as intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) assessment of the return of septal contractility, aortocoronary sinus measurements of enzymes, and cellular functional parameters
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 85

choiceNotes.a: Variation in results is greatest when **only clinical parameters** are used, because the outcome is the sum of all phases.
choiceNotes.c: Time to contracture is a laboratory endpoint (isolated rat hearts); it is species dependent and unknown in humans.
choiceNotes.d: Incision extent and transfusions are intraoperative **influences** on cellular homeostasis, not measures of protection quality.
choiceNotes.e: These are postoperative factors that may impair cellular homeostasis, not assessment parameters.

stem: Which finding about perioperative **myocardial necrosis** is supported by the early clinical studies of conventional cardiac surgery?

choices.text: It was limited to coronary artery bypass grafting
It was absent after simple repair of an uncomplicated atrial septal defect
After isolated aortic valve replacement, about 70% of patients had isoenzymatic evidence of it
It did not occur in children undergoing repair of congenital defects
It did not occur in patients with normal coronary arteries

explanation.text: Myocardial necrosis proved an **important and frequent** complication: in a 1974 isolated AVR study, hospital mortality was only 2%, yet ==70% had isoenzymatic evidence of necrosis== and 15% had ECG evidence of transmural infarction.

explanation.caption: Early evidence that the operation itself damages the myocardium
head: Setting
Finding
rows: Mortality 2%; **15%** ECG transmural MI; **70%** isoenzymatic necrosis
**7%** acute transmural MI after various open operations
High proportion with perioperative transmural MI — soon shown for cardiac surgery **in general**

steps.label: 1975 study
steps.text: Lower early postoperative cardiac output (**inversely proportional**)
Determines early condition and **probability of survival**

explanation.text: Necrosis was found even in patients **convalescing well** — a low mortality does not mean the myocardium was protected.

Although hospital mortality was low (2%), 15% of the patients developed electrocardiographic evidence of transmural myocardial infarction, and 70% developed isoenzymatic evidence of myocardial necrosis.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 86

choiceNotes.a: First publicized with CABG, transmural infarction was soon shown to be a complication of cardiac surgery **in general**.
choiceNotes.b: Even after short, simple uncomplicated ASD repair, adults and children developed isoenzymatic evidence of necrosis.
choiceNotes.d: Necrosis was demonstrated by enzymatic methods in children undergoing surgery for a number of congenital defects.
choiceNotes.e: In 1973 a 7% occurrence of acute transmural MI was documented in patients with **normal coronary arteries**.

stem: Serum **troponin I and T** isoforms after cardiopulmonary bypass were found to be related to which operative variable?

choices.text: The cardiopulmonary bypass flow rate
The degree of systemic hypothermia
The volume of noncoronary collateral flow
The extent of the surgical incision
The duration of ischemic time during cardioplegia

explanation.text: Troponin I and T — **sensitive and somewhat specific** markers of myocardial injury after CPB — were related to ==duration of ischemic time during cardioplegia==.

items: **ECG** criteria for transmural infarction and ischemic changes
**Cardiac-specific enzymes**: concentrations correlate directly with amount of necrotic muscle
**Troponin I and T**: related to ischemic time
**Radionuclide imaging**: presence and extent of perioperative infarction

explanation.text: Isoforms of troponin I and T, sensitive and somewhat specific serum markers of myocardial injury following CPB, were found to be related to duration of ischemic time during cardioplegia
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 86

choiceNotes.a: The source relates troponin isoforms to **ischemic time during cardioplegia**, not to bypass flow rate.
choiceNotes.b: Systemic temperature is not the variable the source links to troponin release; ischemic time is.
choiceNotes.c: Noncoronary collateral flow is not linked to troponin in the source; troponin tracks **ischemic time during cardioplegia**.
choiceNotes.d: Incision extent affects redox homeostasis, but the troponin relation described is with **ischemic time**.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: **Aprikalim** and **pinacidil** were studied as alternatives to conventional cardioplegic arrest. On which principle is this approach based?

choices.text: Membrane hyperpolarization via ATP-sensitive K^+^ channel opening
Hyperkalemic cell membrane depolarization
Calcium channel blockade, as with nifedipine
Scavenging of oxygen-derived free radicals
Procaine-magnesium membrane stabilization

explanation.text: Aprikalim and pinacidil are **K^+^ channel openers**: they arrest the heart by ==membrane hyperpolarization (nearer the resting state)== via ATP-sensitive K^+^ channels, **rather than** hyperkalemic depolarization.

explanation.caption: Pharmacologic approaches in the history of cardioplegia
head: Approach
Example in the source

explanation.text: Standard potassium cardioplegia **depolarizes** the membrane; K^+^ channel openers keep it **hyperpolarized** — opposite membrane states.

In the 1990s Wechsler and colleagues began experiments using concepts of membrane hyperpolarization (nearer the resting state) via adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-sensitive K+ channels rather than hyperkalemic cell membrane depolarization
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 87

choiceNotes.b: Hyperkalemic depolarization is the conventional approach these agents were meant to **replace**.
choiceNotes.c: Nifedipine is the calcium channel blocker whose favorable effect Clark reported; aprikalim and pinacidil are K^+^ channel openers.
choiceNotes.d: Free radical scavengers are superoxide dismutase and catalase, not K^+^ channel openers.
choiceNotes.e: Procaine-magnesium cardioplegia was used by Kirsch’s group; it is not the K-ATP mechanism.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: After aortic unclamping, a surgeon gives an **initially hyperkalemic reperfusate** so that electromechanical quiescence continues for a few minutes into reperfusion. This practice grew from which key observation?

choices.text: Blood is the optimal vehicle for cardioplegic solution
Profound topical cooling with ice slush protects the myocardium
Retrograde infusion is effective in valvar and coronary surgery
Energy supply is replenished rapidly when quiescence continues into reperfusion
Noncoronary collateral flow is usually less than 3% of coronary flow

explanation.text: In 1960 Danforth showed the **rapidity** with which myocardial energy supply is replenished after ischemia ==when electromechanical quiescence is continued for a few minutes into reperfusion==.

steps.text: **1960** Danforth: rapid energy repletion with continued quiescence

steps.label: unused until 1978
steps.text: Buckberg: improved outcome with an **initially hyperkalemic reperfusate** (experimental)

steps.label: then
steps.text: Modified reperfusate; **warm induction** with enriched, modified hyperkalemic blood for **acutely energy-deficient** hearts

steps.label: plus
steps.text: Control of **perfusion pressure** and continued controlled reperfusion until full recovery

explanation.title: Related concept
explanation.text: Sustained potassium arrest reduced metabolic demands by about **85%**, even at normothermia — the basis of Lichtenstein and Salerno’s **warm continuous blood cardioplegia** with minimal potassium.

In 1960, Danforth and colleagues showed the rapidity with which myocardial energy supply is replenished after ischemia when electromechanical quiescence is continued for a few minutes into the reperfusion period.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 87

choiceNotes.a: Buckberg identified blood as the optimal cardioplegic vehicle (1979), but that concerns the arrest solution, not the hyperkalemic reperfusate.
choiceNotes.b: Ice slush (Hufnagel, 1961) was an early cooling method, unrelated to reperfusion strategy.
choiceNotes.c: Retrograde and combined delivery concern the **mode of delivery** of cardioplegia, not continued quiescence during reperfusion.
choiceNotes.e: Collateral flow explains return of activity during clamping in some patients; it is not the basis of hyperkalemic reperfusion.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: In a normal heart with intact circulation, which statement about **transmural myocardial blood flow** is correct?

choices.text: The subendocardial-to-subepicardial flow ratio is normally about 0.5
Subepicardial flow occurs almost exclusively during systole
Subendocardial flow occurs almost exclusively during diastole
The subendocardium consumes oxygen at a lower rate than outer layers
Myocardial flow is independent of tension in the myocardial layers

explanation.text: Subendocardial flow occurs ==almost exclusively during diastole==, because systolic intramyocardial tension closes the coronary branches that pass **perpendicularly** through the myocardium to arborize in the subendocardium.

head: Subepicardium (outer ¼)
Subendocardium (inner ¼)
rows: Flow relative to the other layer

children: Related to wall thickness and size
Depends on endothelium and smooth muscle

explanation.text: This diastolic dependence, plus higher oxygen consumption, explains the **subendocardial vulnerability** in shock, hypertrophy, coronary disease and cardiac surgery.

blood flow to the subendocardial layer occurs almost exclusively during diastole because intramyocardial tension during systole closes the branches of the coronary arteries that pass perpendicularly through the myocardium
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 87

choiceNotes.a: The normal inner-to-outer flow ratio is **1.0 or a little greater**.
choiceNotes.b: Subepicardial flow occurs during **both** systole and diastole.
choiceNotes.d: The subendocardial layer has a **higher** rate of oxygen consumption.
choiceNotes.e: Flow is determined in part by tension in the myocardial layers (related to wall thickness and size).

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: A small heart is decompressed and cooled on **total cardiopulmonary bypass**, still perfused and unclamped. How does the empty state affect **subendocardial perfusion**?

choices.text: It lowers intramyocardial tension and increases subendocardial flow
It has little effect, because coronary flow is maintained by pulsatile pressure
It has little effect, because coronary flow comes antegrade from the left ventricle
It lowers subendocardial resistance, an effect enhanced by ventricular fibrillation
It raises intramyocardial tension and subendocardial resistance, decreasing flow

explanation.text: The empty heart is **smaller**, which ==increases intramyocardial tension and subendocardial vascular resistance== and **decreases** subendocardial flow — especially powerful in the **small** and **hypothermic** heart.

items: Blood enters via the aortic cannula and passes **retrogradely** into the proximal aorta to the coronary ostia
Pulse pressure narrow — **essentially nonpulsatile**; mean pressure variable
Perfusate: **diluted blood** with abnormal physiochemical properties, possible microemboli, altered leukocytes and platelets

explanation.text: An empty, perfused heart on CPB — **even when beating** — is not managed optimally; clinical experience refutes that view.

The heart is usually more or less empty and thus smaller than usual, thereby increasing intramyocardial tension and transmural and subendocardial vascular resistance, and decreasing flow to the subendocardial layer.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 87

choiceNotes.a: The smaller empty heart has **increased**, not decreased, intramyocardial tension.
choiceNotes.b: Arterial pulse pressure on CPB is narrow (**essentially nonpulsatile**).
choiceNotes.c: On total CPB, blood passes **retrogradely** from the aortic cannula into the proximal aorta and coronary ostia.
choiceNotes.d: Ventricular fibrillation **increases** intramyocardial tension still more.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: A patient with severe aortic stenosis and a **markedly hypertrophied** left ventricle is scheduled for valve replacement. Which feature makes this ventricle more susceptible to ischemic and reperfusion damage?

choices.text: Elevated xanthine oxidase and decreased superoxide dismutase levels
Decreased xanthine oxidase and elevated superoxide dismutase levels
Reduced transmural gradients of energy substrate utilization
Delayed onset of ischemic contracture compared with normal hearts
Wall characteristics that make subendocardial reperfusion easier

explanation.text: In hypertrophy, ==xanthine oxidase is markedly elevated== (more free radical generation) and ==superoxide dismutase markedly decreased== (weaker natural defenses).

children: Transmural gradients of substrate utilization **markedly elevated**
Develops **more rapidly** than in normal hearts

explanation.caption: Other hearts the source calls especially vulnerable
head: Heart
Why
rows: Considerably more susceptible to ischemic and reperfusion damage
Highly sensitive to global myocardial ischemia

explanation.text: Xanthine oxidase levels are markedly elevated, increasing the opportunity for the elaboration of oxygen-derived free radicals. Superoxide dismutase levels are markedly decreased, reducing the natural defenses against oxygen-derived free radicals.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 88

choiceNotes.b: This reverses the source: xanthine oxidase is **elevated** and superoxide dismutase **decreased**.
choiceNotes.c: Transmural gradients of energy substrate utilization are markedly **elevated** in hypertrophy.
choiceNotes.d: Contracture develops **more rapidly** in hypertrophied than in normal hearts.
choiceNotes.e: The hypertrophied wall makes subendocardial reperfusion **more difficult** than normal.

stem: The heart of a patient with **chronic heart failure** is described as chronically depleted in **energy charge**. Which statement about energy charge is correct?

choices.text: It is normally 1.0 and falls to 0.85 when nucleotides are all ADP
It is normally 0.85 and would be 1.0 if nucleotides were all AMP
It is normally 0.5 and reflects the myocardial glycogen content
It is normally 0.85 and would be 1.0 if nucleotides were all ATP
It is normally 0.85 and would be 1.0 if nucleotides were all adenosine

explanation.text: Energy charge = energy-producing capacity of the **adenine nucleotide** mix in mitochondria and cytoplasm: ==normally 0.85==; **1.0** if present only as ATP; **0.0** if only as AMP.
The failing heart starts **already depleted** and is particularly susceptible to further acute depletion during ischemia and reperfusion.
Normally, it is 0.85. It would be 1.0 if the nucleotides were present only as ATP but 0.0 if they were present only as adenosine monophosphate.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 88

choiceNotes.a: Normal energy charge is **0.85**; 1.0 applies only if all nucleotides were ATP.
choiceNotes.b: All-AMP gives an energy charge of **0.0**, not 1.0.
choiceNotes.c: Normal value is 0.85, and it describes adenine nucleotides, not glycogen.
choiceNotes.e: The value of 1.0 corresponds to nucleotides present only as **ATP**.

stem: During aortic cross-clamping in a patient with **cyanotic congenital heart disease**, the heart repeatedly resumes electromechanical activity despite cardioplegia. Which explanation fits the source?

choices.text: Early recovery of specialized conduction cells ahead of myocytes
Calcium influx typical of uncontrolled reperfusion
Noncoronary collateral flow, enough to restart activity but not to prevent ischemia
Normal noncoronary collateral flow, which is about one-third of coronary flow
A hyperpolarized membrane state produced by potassium cardioplegia

explanation.text: Even with the aorta clamped, **noncoronary collateral flow** from **mediastinal arteries** continues. In some patients it is ==sufficient to initiate electromechanical activity but insufficient to prevent continuing and important ischemia==.

head: Noncoronary collateral flow
rows: Cyanotic congenital heart disease, advanced ischemic heart disease, extensive pericarditis, other conditions

explanation.text: “Global” ischemia is not truly zero flow — but collateral flow that restarts the heart still leaves it **ischemic**.
coronary collateral flow may be sufficient to initiate electromechanical activity in the heart rendered quiescent by cardioplegia but insufficient to prevent continuing and important ischemia
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 88

choiceNotes.a: Specialized conduction cells may be the **last** to recover, not the first.
choiceNotes.b: Calcium influx is a feature of reperfusion injury; the heart here is still clamped.
choiceNotes.d: Noncoronary collateral flow is generally **less than 3%** of total coronary flow.
choiceNotes.e: Hyperkalemic cardioplegia **depolarizes** the membrane; hyperpolarization is the K^+^ channel opener concept.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass
source.loc: p. 88, Vulnerability of the Diseased Heart

stem: Why is a period of **global myocardial ischemia** (aortic clamping) commonly accepted for intracardiac procedures?

choices.text: Cardiac operations cannot be performed on a perfused beating heart
It removes the need for any special myocardial management
A perfused fibrillating heart is the bloodless field of choice
Ischemia and reperfusion cannot be controlled as separate events
A bloodless, quiescent heart best allows precise repair without air embolization

explanation.text: A precise, complete procedure **without air embolization** is most likely when the heart is ==bloodless and mechanically quiescent== — conditions provided by global myocardial ischemia.

steps.label: requires
steps.text: Appropriate **myocardial management** to limit ischemic damage

explanation.text: The surgeon has a unique opportunity to **control ischemia and reperfusion separately** — which is why the chapter discusses them separately.
the probability of a precise and complete surgical procedure without air embolization is greatest when the heart is bloodless and mechanically quiescent
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 88

choiceNotes.a: Operations **can** be performed with the heart perfused and beating, fibrillating or in diastolic arrest.
choiceNotes.b: Global ischemia **necessitates** appropriate myocardial management to limit damage.
choiceNotes.c: The optimal field is bloodless **and mechanically quiescent**; a perfused fibrillating heart is neither.
choiceNotes.d: The surgeon has a **unique opportunity** to control and influence each separately.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: After the onset of global myocardial ischemia, how quickly does the myocardium switch from **aerobic to anaerobic glycolysis**?

choices.text: Within about 15 minutes
Within seconds
After about 20 minutes
After about 1 hour
Only after about 6 hours

explanation.text: Nayler and Elz stress the **rapidity** of the chain of ischemic events: the switch from aerobic to anaerobic glycolysis occurs ==within seconds== of onset of ischemia.

explanation.caption: Times stated in the source
head: Time
Event
rows: Loss of control of **sarcolemmal membrane permeability** begins
Compatible with myocyte survival in other evidence

explanation.text: There is **extreme heterogeneity** among cells (and by implication among hearts) in the rate of progression of ischemic damage — no single safe time applies to every heart.
the switch from aerobic to anaerobic glycolysis occurs within seconds of onset of ischemia
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 88

choiceNotes.a: Fifteen minutes is when loss of control of sarcolemmal membrane permeability **begins**.
choiceNotes.c: Twenty minutes of normothermic ischemia is the shortest time reported for **subendocardial necrosis**.
choiceNotes.d: One hour is not the time the source gives for this metabolic switch, which occurs within seconds.
choiceNotes.e: Six hours is the longest normothermic ischemia reported **compatible with cell survival**.

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes **myocardial stunning** from **myocardial hibernation**?

choices.text: Stunning is a chronic state with low perfusion and low contraction
Hibernation follows brief ischemia and resolves after reperfusion
Stunning is a perfusion/contraction mismatch; hibernation is a match, both low
Stunning reflects reduced Ca^2+^ transients; hibernation reflects reduced myofilament Ca^2+^ responsiveness
Stunning, unlike hibernation, requires myocardial necrosis

explanation.text: Stunning = ==perfusion/contraction **mismatch**== (flow restored, contractility still low). Hibernation = perfusion/contraction **match** (both low).

head: Stunning
Hibernation
rows: After acutely diminished flow + adequate reperfusion

explanation.text: The difference between stunned and hibernating segments **may be vague** clinically.
**S**tunned = **S**plit (flow and function mismatched); **H**ibernating = **H**and in hand (both low).
If stunning is characterized as a perfusion/contraction mismatch, hibernation is a perfusion/contraction match; in the latter, both are low.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 88

choiceNotes.a: The chronic state with both perfusion and contraction low is **hibernation**.
choiceNotes.b: Stunning, not hibernation, follows diminished flow with adequate reperfusion; hibernation is chronic.
choiceNotes.d: Reversed: reduced Ca^2+^ transients are proposed for **hibernation**, reduced myofilament responsiveness for **stunning**.
choiceNotes.e: Stunning is dysfunction **in the absence of** myocardial necrosis.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: It has been suggested that myocardial stunning results from abnormal energy transduction secondary to **depletion of high-energy phosphates**. Which observation argues against this?

choices.text: Stunned myocardium has a high, not low, oxygen consumption
Superoxide dismutase and catalase given before ischemia restore contraction
Excess intracellular calcium soon leaves cells after short ischemia
Stunned myocardium responds to inotropic stimulation
Stunning begins in the subendocardium and progresses outward

explanation.text: Stunned myocardium ==responds to inotropic stimulation==, indicating **adequate ATP** for active contraction — against the high-energy phosphate depletion theory.

explanation.caption: Proposed causes of stunning and the evidence
head: Hypothesis
Evidence in the source
rows: **Does not appear** to be the cause
Possible; must be reconciled with calcium leaving cells after short ischemia

explanation.text: Each choice is a real observation — match it to the **hypothesis it addresses**. High O~2~ consumption refutes the **reduced-consumption** theory, not the ATP theory.
Stunned myocardium, however, responds to inotropic stimulation, indicating the presence of adequate ATP to produce active contraction.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 88

choiceNotes.a: High oxygen consumption refutes the **reduced oxygen consumption** hypothesis, not the ATP-depletion theory.
choiceNotes.b: This supports the **free radical** mechanism; it does not address ATP availability.
choiceNotes.c: This challenges the **calcium/EC coupling** hypothesis.
choiceNotes.e: This describes the **pattern** of stunning (like necrosis), not evidence about ATP.

stem: In experimental studies, which agents given **before** an ischemic period resulted in nearly full restoration of contractile indices on reperfusion, compared with prolonged depression in controls?

choices.text: Xanthine oxidase and hypoxanthine
Iron and hydrogen peroxide
Nifedipine and procaine
Calcium and potassium
Superoxide dismutase and catalase

explanation.text: **Superoxide dismutase and catalase** (free radical scavengers) before ischemia ==nearly fully restored contractile indices== on reperfusion in experiments.
Free radical release occurs to a major degree in the **first few minutes of reperfusion** — the early reperfusion period is the target.

Experimentally, introduction of superoxide dismutase and catalase (free radical scavengers) before an ischemic period results in nearly full restoration of contractile indices upon reperfusion, compared with prolonged depression in controls.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 89

choiceNotes.a: Xanthine oxidase acting on hypoxanthine **generates** free radicals at reperfusion.
choiceNotes.b: Iron converts superoxide into damaging hydroxyl radicals; hydrogen peroxide is itself a free radical species.
choiceNotes.c: Nifedipine (calcium channel blocker) and procaine (Kirsch solution) are other historical protective agents, not the scavengers tested here.
choiceNotes.d: Calcium influx is a proposed **cause** of stunning, not a protective agent here.

stem: A surgeon plans a **short aortic cross-clamp time**, well below that expected to cause myocyte death, and asks whether full myocardial management techniques are needed. What does the chapter advise?

choices.text: Use them, because stunning can follow even brief ischemia and they likely prevent it
Omit them, because stunning occurs only with ischemia long enough to cause necrosis
Omit them, because stunning reflects persistently impaired coronary flow
Omit them unless the ventricle is hypertrophied or failing
Use them only during reperfusion, because ischemia alone does not stun

explanation.text: Techniques designed to minimize necrosis are probably **effective against stunning** too, so ==use them even when ischemia is shorter than that expected to cause cell death==.

steps.label: may last
steps.text: Minutes to **many days** → prolonged postoperative low cardiac output

items: Stunning is a form of myocardial cell damage caused by **ischemia and reperfusion**
Begins in the **subendocardium** and progresses outward; recovery proceeds in reverse
Not explained by continuing postischemic impairment of coronary flow or reserve

explanation.text: these techniques should be used even when the period of global myocardial ischemia is less than that anticipated to result in myocardial cell death
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 89

choiceNotes.b: Stunning **can follow even brief periods** of myocardial ischemia, without necrosis.
choiceNotes.c: Stunning does not appear to result from continuing postischemic impairment of coronary flow or coronary reserve.
choiceNotes.d: The advice applies generally, not only to vulnerable hearts.
choiceNotes.e: Stunning is caused by **ischemia and reperfusion**; techniques should be applied to the ischemic period as well.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass
Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: Early in global myocardial ischemia, which event removes the **building blocks needed for ATP repletion** from the myocyte?

choices.text: Leakage of fatty acid acyl-CoA derivatives out of the cell
Loss of adenosine, inosine and other nucleotides from the cell
Stimulation of anaerobic glycolysis by intracellular alkalosis
Increased fatty acid utilization by the mitochondria
Accumulation of glycogen granules in the cytoplasm

explanation.text: **Adenosine, inosine and other nucleotides** — products of ATP catabolism and ==building blocks for ATP repletion== — leave the cell as energy charge and glycogen fall.

steps.text: Oxidative phosphorylation declines; some ATP from inefficient **anaerobic glycolysis**
Lactate + protons → **acidosis**, which suppresses anaerobic glycolysis
↓ Energy charge and glycogen; **nucleotide precursors leave the cell**

explanation.text: Early ultrastructure: only **loss of glycogen granules** and some intracellular and organelle swelling.
adenosine, inosine, and other nucleotides that are the results of ATP catabolism and the building blocks for ATP repletion leave the cell
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 89

choiceNotes.a: Fatty acid acyl-CoA derivatives **accumulate** within the cell.
choiceNotes.c: Intracellular **acidosis** develops and **suppresses** anaerobic glycolysis.
choiceNotes.d: Fatty acid utilization is **rapidly reduced**.
choiceNotes.e: Early ultrastructural change is **loss** of glycogen granules.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: Which statement about **ischemic myocardial contracture** is correct?

choices.text: It first develops in the subepicardium
It develops more slowly in hypertrophied hearts
It first develops in the subendocardium because of its higher metabolic rate
Its onset is hastened by hypothermia
Its timing is similar across species and well defined in humans

explanation.text: Contracture signals ATP depleted to a **critically low** level; it ==first develops in the subendocardium== because of its **higher metabolic rate** and faster ATP depletion.

children: Unknown but probably long in humans
Differs in crystalloid vs blood-perfused rat hearts

explanation.text: Time-to-contracture, a key endpoint in **isolated rat heart** studies, cannot be transferred directly to human hearts.
Contracture first develops in the subendocardium because of its higher metabolic rate and consequent more rapid depletion of ATP.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 89

choiceNotes.a: Contracture first develops in the **subendocardium**.
choiceNotes.b: Contracture develops **more rapidly** in hypertrophied hearts.
choiceNotes.d: Hypothermia **delays** the onset of contracture.
choiceNotes.e: Time to contracture is **highly species dependent** and unknown in humans.

source.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: After prolonged myocardial ischemia, flow through the large epicardial coronary arteries appears adequate, yet **microcirculatory flow is impaired** (no-reflow). Which combination of mechanisms is described?

choices.text: Large-vessel endothelial necrosis with epicardial coronary spasm
Excess endothelial relaxing factor with capillary dilation
Reduced leukocyte adhesion molecules with platelet inhibition
Decreased vasomotor tone with collapse of the coronary sinus
Endothelial swelling, neutrophil accumulation, microthrombosis and increased vasomotor tone

explanation.text: No-reflow = ==endothelial swelling, accumulation of neutrophils, microthrombosis and increased vasomotor tone== → impaired microcirculatory flow despite apparently adequate flow in large epicardial arteries.

steps.text: Swelling, platelet activation, microthrombosis, ↑ vasomotor tone
Neutrophils infiltrate myocardium: lipid peroxidation, membrane degradation, **calcium overload**, EC uncoupling

explanation.text: No-reflow is seen after prolonged ischemia, particularly in the **inner half** of the myocardium.

In children, **IL-8** is liberated during CPB, and P-selectin, E-selectin and ICAM are expressed in myocardial biopsies during cardioplegic arrest in infants; how much this contributes to dysfunction is **unknown**.
This contributes to impaired microcirculatory flow, despite what appears to be adequate perfusion through the large epicardial arteries.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 90

choiceNotes.a: The endothelium of large coronary arteries appears **little affected**; the problem is microcirculatory.
choiceNotes.b: Vasomotor tone is **increased**, not decreased by excess relaxing factor.
choiceNotes.c: Activated endothelium **induces** leukocyte adhesion molecules, and platelets are **activated**.
choiceNotes.d: Vasomotor tone is **increased** in no-reflow.

stem: Neutrophil adhesion to hypoxic, activated coronary endothelium is a multistep process. Which interaction forms the **firm bond**?

choices.text: Neutrophil integrins (CD11/18) with endothelial ICAM-1
Endothelial P-selectin with passing neutrophils
Endothelial E-selectin with passing neutrophils
Endothelial tissue factor with circulating platelets
Endothelial NF-κB with neutrophil interleukin-8

explanation.text: The **firm bond** forms between ==integrins on the leukocyte (CD11/18)== and endothelial adhesion molecules (**ICAM-1**, VCAM, PECAM).

steps.text: Hypoxia → Weibel-Palade bodies release **P-selectin**; NF-κB activated

steps.label: NF-κB promotes
steps.text: Transcription of E-selectin, ICAM, tissue factor, IL-8, IL-1

explanation.text: Selectins mediate **rolling** (low-affinity); integrin–ICAM binding mediates **firm** adhesion.

neutrophils become activated, and a firm bond forms between integrins on the leukocyte surface (i.e., CD 11/18) and adhesion molecules on the endothelium (i.e., ICAM-1, vascular cell adhesion molecule, platelet-endothelial cell adhesion molecule)
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 90

choiceNotes.b: P-selectin forms **low-affinity** bonds that cause rolling and slowing, not the firm bond.
choiceNotes.c: E-selectin, like P-selectin, mediates low-affinity rolling.
choiceNotes.d: Tissue factor is a product transcribed under NF-κB; it is not the firm neutrophil bond.
choiceNotes.e: NF-κB is an endothelial transcription factor; IL-8 is one of its products, not an adhesion bond.

stem: Five minutes after initially hyperkalemic reperfusion, the ventricle responds strongly to **direct ventricular pacing** but is quiescent with atrial pacing; sinus rhythm appears some minutes later. Which interpretation fits the source?

choices.text: Necrosis of specialized conduction cells, needing permanent pacing
Conduction-cell stunning, recovering later than the myocytes
Myocyte stunning, with conduction cells recovering first
Noncoronary collateral flow reactivating the ventricle only
Well-defined reperfusion injury of conduction cells

explanation.text: Specialized conduction cells become nonfunctional **early** during ischemia, and their recovery may take ==longer than recovery of myocytes== — a form of **stunning rather than necrosis**.

steps.text: **~5 min**: ventricle responds to **direct ventricular pacing**; quiescent with atrial pacing or no pacing

explanation.caption: AV conduction after blood cardioplegia + uncontrolled normokalemic reperfusion
head: Finding
Detail
rows: **Third-degree** AV block persisting up to **2 months** gave way to sinus rhythm

explanation.text: This remains **speculation** awaiting validation; sensitivity of conduction fibers to chemical components of the cardioplegic infusate is an alternative explanation. Little is known about **reperfusion** injury of conduction cells.
This appears to be a form of specialized conduction cell stunning rather than necrosis because these disappear by the time of hospital discharge in most of the patients in whom it had developed.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 90

choiceNotes.a: AV disturbances disappear by discharge in most patients, even third-degree block up to 2 months — stunning, not necrosis.
choiceNotes.c: Myocytes respond (to ventricular pacing) **before** conduction tissue, which may be the last to recover.
choiceNotes.d: Collateral flow during clamping is unrelated to this post-reperfusion pacing pattern.
choiceNotes.e: Little specific information is available about reperfusion injury to the specialized conduction cells.

stem: After a long ischemic period followed by **uncontrolled reperfusion**, the heart becomes rigid and fibrillating (“stone heart”). Which statement is correct?

choices.text: It always means the point of no return has been passed
It is a massive infarction that is complete before reperfusion begins
It may be regional, typically the basilar left ventricle and subendocardium
It typically spares the subendocardium and involves the apical subepicardium
Histology shows a preserved myofibrillar pattern without contraction bands

explanation.text: Stone heart may involve only some regions — ==typically the basilar portion of the left ventricle and the subendocardium== — and is, at least sometimes, **capable of recovery**.

explanation.title: Response to uncontrolled reperfusion, by severity

steps.label: more severe
steps.text: **Reperfusion arrhythmias** (VT, VF) — more with longer and larger ischemia

items: Approaches the critical “point of no return” but has not necessarily reached it

explanation.title: Uncontrolled reperfusion
explanation.text: Reperfusion by **unmodified blood** without control of **pressure or flow**.
The stone heart phenomenon may involve only some regions of the heart, typically the basilar portion of the left ventricle and the subendocardium.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 91

choiceNotes.a: It may have **approached** the point of no return, but is at least under some circumstances capable of recovery.
choiceNotes.b: Stone heart has been confirmed to be a massive infarction **developing during reperfusion**.
choiceNotes.d: It typically involves the basilar left ventricle and the **subendocardium**.
choiceNotes.e: Histology shows **disruption** of the myofibrillar pattern and evident contraction bands.

stem: What causes the **stiffness** of cardiac muscle produced by uncontrolled reperfusion after a period of ischemia?

choices.text: Critical ATP depletion during ischemia alone
Hyperkalemic depolarization from residual cardioplegia
Accumulation of fatty acid acyl-CoA in the myocytes
Massive calcium influx into mitochondria and cytoplasm, with edema and capillary disruption
Neutrophil plugging of the large epicardial coronary arteries

explanation.text: Reperfusion stiffness is caused by ==massive influx of calcium into mitochondria and cytoplasm== of myocytes, plus **edema** and **capillary disruption**.

explanation.center: Reperfusion of ischemic myocardium (Jennings and Reimer)

children: Accelerated **creatine kinase** washout early in reperfusion

explanation.text: Many events are **well underway within 1 or 2 minutes** of uncontrolled reperfusion — the first minutes matter most.
Ischemic **contracture** (ATP depletion during ischemia) is not the same as reperfusion **stiffness** (calcium influx, edema, capillary disruption).

Stiffness of cardiac muscle resulting from uncontrolled reperfusion after a period of ischemia is caused by the massive influx of calcium into mitochondria and cytoplasm of myocytes, as well as by edema and capillary disruption.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 91

choiceNotes.a: Critical ATP depletion during ischemia produces **ischemic contracture**, a different process.
choiceNotes.b: The source does not attribute reperfusion stiffness to cardioplegic depolarization.
choiceNotes.c: Acyl-CoA accumulation is an early **ischemic** metabolic change, not the cause of reperfusion stiffness.
choiceNotes.e: Neutrophils plug **capillaries**; stiffness is attributed to calcium influx, edema and capillary disruption.

stem: Which statement about **neutrophils** in myocardial reperfusion injury is correct?

choices.text: They are activated only by the bypass circuit, not by the ischemic myocardium
They plug myocardial capillaries because of large size and adherence to damaged endothelium
Their arachidonic acid metabolites cause vasodilation and inhibit platelets
They act mainly as scavengers of oxygen-derived free radicals
They sustain reperfusion injury but play no role in initiating it

explanation.text: Neutrophils ==plug myocardial capillaries== because of their **large size** and **active adherence** to ischemically damaged endothelium.

steps.text: Locally generated in ischemic myocardium: chemotactic factors, activated endothelium, **C5a**, cytokines

branches.label: release
branches.text: Arachidonic acid metabolites → endothelial injury, **vasoconstriction**, **platelet aggregation**

explanation.text: During reperfusion, certain **leukotrienes** are also released from platelets and endothelial cells.
Neutrophils plug myocardial capillaries as reperfusion continues because of their large size and active adherence to ischemically damaged endothelial cells.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 91

choiceNotes.a: Activating factors (chemotactic factors, C5a, cytokines) are **generated locally in ischemic myocardium**.
choiceNotes.c: Arachidonic acid metabolites cause **vasoconstriction** and **platelet aggregation**, plus endothelial injury.
choiceNotes.d: Neutrophils **release** large amounts of oxygen-derived free radicals.
choiceNotes.e: Neutrophils play an important role in **initiating and sustaining** reperfusion injury.

stem: In the chain reaction of oxygen-derived free radicals at reperfusion, what converts relatively innocuous **superoxide** into highly damaging **hydroxyl radicals**?

choices.text: Iron
Superoxide dismutase
Catalase
Glutathione peroxidase
Xanthine dehydrogenase

explanation.text: ==Iron== plays a key role in converting relatively innocuous **superoxide** radicals into highly damaging **hydroxyl** radicals.

explanation.caption: Who does what with oxygen-derived free radicals
head: Agent
Action
rows: Catalyzes reoxygenation of hypoxanthine and xanthine → superoxide at reperfusion

items: Free radicals have **unpaired electrons**: superoxide (O~2~^-^), hydrogen peroxide (H~2~O~2~), hydroxyl radical (OH^-^)
Normal sources: mitochondria (95% of O~2~ consumption), cytoplasm, endothelium (xanthine oxidase), activated neutrophils

explanation.text: As part of this chain reaction, iron plays a key role in converting relatively innocuous superoxide radicals into highly damaging hydroxyl radicals.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 91

choiceNotes.b: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to **hydrogen peroxide and water** — a defense.
choiceNotes.c: Catalase metabolizes hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen.
choiceNotes.d: Glutathione peroxidase, like catalase, metabolizes hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen.
choiceNotes.e: Xanthine dehydrogenase is the normal enzyme that is **converted to xanthine oxidase** during ischemia.

stem: Which combination of changes during ischemia **primes** the myocardium for a burst of oxygen-derived free radicals at the onset of uncontrolled reperfusion?

choices.text: Rising superoxide dismutase, falling hypoxanthine, xanthine oxidase → dehydrogenase
Rising superoxide dismutase, rising hypoxanthine, xanthine oxidase → dehydrogenase
Falling superoxide dismutase, falling hypoxanthine, xanthine oxidase → dehydrogenase
Falling superoxide dismutase, rising hypoxanthine, xanthine dehydrogenase → oxidase
Unchanged superoxide dismutase, rising hypoxanthine, loss of xanthine oxidase

explanation.text: Ischemia ==decreases superoxide dismutase==, ==increases hypoxanthine and xanthine== (ATP catabolites), and ==converts xanthine dehydrogenase to xanthine oxidase==.

steps.label: attack
steps.text: **Peroxidation** of unsaturated fatty acids in membranes

explanation.text: The direction of conversion is **dehydrogenase → oxidase** (ischemia creates the radical-generating enzyme).
Ischemia progressively decreases the cellular levels of the scavenger superoxide dismutase and also increases metabolic end products of ATP catabolism, such as hypoxanthine and xanthine.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 91

choiceNotes.a: Ischemia **decreases** SOD, **increases** hypoxanthine, and converts dehydrogenase **to** oxidase.
choiceNotes.b: SOD **falls** during ischemia, and the conversion is dehydrogenase → oxidase.
choiceNotes.c: Hypoxanthine **rises** (ATP catabolite), and the conversion is dehydrogenase → oxidase.
choiceNotes.e: SOD progressively **decreases**, and xanthine oxidase is **formed**, not lost.

stem: One hour after reperfusion of an ischemic region, myocytes surrounding a necrotic area are viable and contracting, yet several hours later they have become necrotic. What best explains this?

choices.text: Delayed closure of arterioles and capillaries causing no-reflow
Reperfusion injury of the endothelium of large coronary arteries
Endothelial damage completed during ischemia, before reperfusion
Late contracture from ATP depletion in the subepicardium
Persistent noncoronary collateral flow after unclamping

explanation.text: Viable border myocytes can die over hours from ==delayed closure of coronary arterioles and capillaries== — the **no-reflow** phenomenon.

head: Vessel level
Effect of ischemia-reperfusion
rows: **Profoundly** affected; dysfunction develops rapidly with onset of reperfusion

items: Damage **minimal after ischemia itself**; incited almost exclusively by **reperfusion**
Endothelial cells swell; activated neutrophils and platelets aggregate and adhere

explanation.text: This damage appears minimal after ischemia itself but is incited almost exclusively by reperfusion.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 91

choiceNotes.b: The endothelial cells of **large** coronary arteries appear little affected.
choiceNotes.c: Microvascular endothelial damage appears **minimal after ischemia itself** and is incited almost exclusively by reperfusion.
choiceNotes.d: Contracture reflects critical ATP depletion and starts in the **subendocardium**; it does not explain delayed death of reperfused border cells.
choiceNotes.e: Collateral flow during clamping does not explain delayed necrosis after reperfusion; delayed microvascular closure does.

stem: During uncontrolled reperfusion, coronary vascular resistance rises progressively. Which mechanism does the source describe?

choices.text: Enhanced endothelium-dependent relaxation to acetylcholine and bradykinin
Impaired endothelium-dependent relaxation, exposing smooth muscle to constrictors
Shrinkage of myocardial cells narrowing the intramyocardial vessels
Low wall tension letting coronary vessels collapse
Injury limited to the endothelium of large epicardial arteries

explanation.text: Reperfusion injury ==severely impairs endothelium-dependent relaxation== (to neutrophils, platelets, thrombin, acetylcholine, bradykinin); exposed **smooth muscle** then contracts to additional mediators.
These events are particularly damaging after **prolonged (> 24 hours) cardiac preservation**, as may eventually be required for transplantation.
In addition, with damage to endothelial cells, smooth muscle beneath the cells is exposed, allowing additional mediators to induce direct smooth muscle contraction.
explanation.ref: Chapter 3: Myocardial Management During Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 92

choiceNotes.a: These endothelium-dependent relaxations are severely **impaired**, not enhanced.
choiceNotes.c: Vessels are compressed by myocardial cell **swelling**, not shrinkage.
choiceNotes.d: Vessels are compressed by areas with **high** wall tension.
choiceNotes.e: Large coronary artery endothelium is little affected; the **microvasculature** is profoundly affected.
